newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Upton attacks compulsory superannuation.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Upton attacks compulsory superannuation.

text.p: National Party Environment Minister Simon Upton on Thursday attacked compulsory superannuation, due to be put to a referendum in New Zealand in September.

"I am firmly opposed to a compulsory super savings scheme. I think our current arrangements are not too bad and certainly there is no pressing case to create a compulsory scheme on top of the taxpayer-funded scheme," Upton said in a speech to parliament.
He said it was a myth that more savings would generate more secure retirement incomes in the future, as money could only be a claim on the available resources.
"It is the the future wealth and output of the economy that matters," he said.
"The economy's ability to pay is the key issue. How that payout is broken down between taxes and dividends is a secondary matter."
He said it was also a myth that New Zealand's savings were inadequate, because the country had massive fiscal supluses and excellent levels of corporate profitability and reinvestment.

Upton, seen as the intellectual conscience of the conservative wing of the party, was the first cabinet minister to declare his position since the government announced on Tuesday that the referendum would be held by postal ballot in September.
He disputed the current scheme could not be afforded, and said "the sums were not impossible" after 2016 as an ageing population increased its claim on the economy.
He said New Zealand was as close to intergenerational equity as any country.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Wednesday said he would support compulsory superannuation if the right scheme was proposed.
The National-New Zealand First coalition government agreed to hold a referendum on compulsory superannuation during their coalition talks.

A scheme to make everyone contribute a portion of income to an individual pension savings scheme -- initially three percent in 1998/99, rising to eight percent by 2002 -- was championed by New Zealand First and opposed by National during last year's election campaign.
The government has said it would consider itself bound by the result of the referendum if it was approved by a simple majority of those voting, irrespective of voter turnout.

A core group of officials, including a private sector person, has been established to design the scheme, drawing on the superannuation policy announced by New Zealand First, and the principles outlined by the Todd Taskforce on private provision for retirement.
The coalition government will remain neutral on the proposal and each MP is entitled to argue for or against it. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
